stem.text: Using the substitution u = coshx, find ∫ sinh3x dx.

points.text: ∫ sinh2x du = ∫ (u2 – 1) du; applies correct identity sinh2u = cosh2u – 1 to find integral in terms of u

explanation.text: sinh³x = sinh²x · sinhx, and the substitution u = coshx has du = sinhx dx, so the lone sinhx pairs with dx. That leaves sinh²x to rewrite in terms of u using sinh²x = cosh²x – 1 = u² – 1, turning the whole integral into a polynomial in u.

reasoningChain: Split sinh³x = sinh²x · sinhx so the extra sinhx matches du = sinhx dx.
Rewrite sinh²x using the identity cosh²x – sinh²x = 1, giving sinh²x = u² – 1.
Integrate the resulting polynomial (u² – 1) du directly.
Substitute back u = coshx to express the answer in terms of x.

inferredMistakes.text: Using the identity sinh²x = cosh²x + 1 (wrong sign), which comes from confusing the hyperbolic identity cosh²x – sinh²x = 1 with the trig identity sin²x + cos²x = 1.

stem.text: Find the particular solution of the differential equation
given that y = 0 when x = ln(1/3). Give your answer in the form y = f(x).

points.text: e∫cothx dx = eln sinhx = sinhx; finds integrating factor
d/dx(y sinhx) = sinh3x; correct form on LHS and attempt to integrate RHS
y sinhx = (1/3)cosh3x – coshx + C; integrates RHS using their part (a). For M1, their answer to (a) must be of the correct form acosh3x + bcoshx with a,b non-zero
0 = (1/3)(5/3)3 – 5/3 + C ⇒ C = 10/81; substitutes initial conditions. M0 if expression incorrectly manipulated before substitution, e.g. not all terms divided by sinhx

markScheme.note: x = ln(1/3) gives coshx = (e^x + e^{-x})/2 = (1/3 + 3)/2 = 5/3, which the MS uses directly when substituting the initial condition.

explanation.text: This is a first-order linear ODE dy/dx + P(x)y = Q(x) with P(x) = cothx, solved by the integrating factor method: multiply through by e^∫P dx so the left side becomes the derivative of a product. Since ∫cothx dx = ln(sinhx), the integrating factor is sinhx.

Once multiplied by sinhx, the right side sinh²x·sinhx = sinh³x is exactly the integral computed in part (a), so the two parts of this question are deliberately linked — reusing (a)'s result avoids redoing that integration.
x = ln(1/3) needs converting to a numeric value of coshx before it can be substituted: coshx = (e^x + e^{-x})/2, and with e^x = 1/3, e^{-x} = 3, this gives coshx = (1/3 + 3)/2 = 5/3.

reasoningChain: Identify the ODE as first-order linear in y, with P(x) = cothx.
Find the integrating factor e^∫cothx dx = e^{ln sinhx} = sinhx.
Multiply the whole equation by sinhx so the LHS becomes d/dx(y·sinhx), and the RHS becomes sinh²x·sinhx = sinh³x.
Integrate both sides: the RHS integral is exactly part (a)'s result.
Convert x = ln(1/3) into coshx = 5/3, substitute y=0 to find the constant of integration.
Divide through by sinhx (i.e. multiply by cosechx) to isolate y = f(x).

inferredMistakes.text: Substituting x = ln(1/3) directly as a numeric x-value into cosh/sinh expressions without first converting to the actual value of coshx or sinhx, leading to an unevaluated or incorrect constant C.
Dividing only some terms of the equation y sinhx = (1/3)cosh³x – coshx + C by sinhx when isolating y, rather than every term, which the guidance on point 4 specifically warns about.

issues.note: Part (a) is an integration technique (chapter 4) while part (b) is a differential equation (chapter 6) that reuses part (a)'s result; the two parts touch different chapters so this is filed as cross-topic under chapter 6 (differential equations), since part (b) carries the larger mark allocation (7 of 11).
